question: to the Commission Marion Maréchal (ECR), Nicolas Bay (ECR), Laurence Trochu (ECR), Guillaume Peltier (ECR), Christophe Gomart (PPE), Anne-Sophie Frigout (PfE), Waldemar Buda (ECR), Fabrice Leggeri (PfE), Diana Iovanovici Şoşoacă (NI) Subject:

In a recent letter reported in the press (April 2026), Ursula von der Leyen indicated that the Commission was in favour of revising the Fuel Quality Directive, which, notably, imposes a 10 % limit on the incorporation of bioethanol in petrol (E10) sold to consumers. This limit hinders the development of vehicles compatible with petrol with higher incorporation rates (E20, for example). Increasing this limit would strengthen the European biofuel sector and its agricultural and industrial jobs, encourage manufacturers to adopt these alternative solutions, and contribute to the security of energy supply in Europe. However, this potential revision has not yet been the subject of any official communication from the Commission. The Commission is therefore invited to answer the following questions: 1.
Does it intend to present a proposal amending the Fuel Quality Directive in the near future? If so, according to what timetable?

Given that the Renewable Energy Directive III stipulates that up to 29 % of the energy in transport fuels must come from renewable sources by 2030, what additional measures is it planning to take to develop ethanol production and achieve this ambitious target?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.9.2026) The Fuel Quality Directive1 sets minimum quality requirements for petrol and diesel fuels placed on the EU market with the aim to establish a single fuel market. Currently, the maximum permitted ethanol content in petrol is set at 10% (E10). The Commission acknowledges the role that higher biofuel blends can play to decarbonise the existing vehicles fleets. In the context of the revision of the fuels-related policy framework, the Commission will look into the possibility to enable the higher blends, E20 for example, taking into account possible issues related to engines compatibility as well as the need to incentivise investments in advanced biofuels. Under the Renewable Energy Directive2, it is for Member States, in line with the principle of subsidiarity, to decide how to meet the 2030 transport target. The Commission continues to support all renewable transport solutions, such as certified biofuel feedstocks, advancing electrification and strengthening the overall framework for renewable energy in transport.
